clue.text: It may be available if some hundreds are already taken by a politician of an otherwise retiring disposition

definitions.text: It may be available if some hundreds are already taken by a politician of an otherwise retiring disposition

parts.words: It may be available if some hundreds are already taken by a politician of an otherwise retiring disposition
parts.note: an MP cannot simply resign, so takes a nominal Crown office; if the Chiltern Hundreds are already held, this other sinecure is used

explanation.surface: A shy politician finds that some hundreds of something have already been snapped up.
explanation.walkthrough: British MPs leave the Commons by accepting a paid Crown office: the Chiltern Hundreds or this Yorkshire manor, used alternately. 'Retiring' means resigning, not shy.
explanation.definitionFit: This Crown stewardship is the nominal office, besides the Chiltern Hundreds, that a resigning member of Parliament accepts.

indicators.note: the words before are the raw material used to make something new, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A gardener explains that flowers are his means of making a living.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' signals that ONE and MEANS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Windflowers of the buttercup family, grown for their bright blooms.

clue.text: To do this is hardly to one's credit

definitions.text: To do this is hardly to one's credit

parts.words: To do this is hardly to one's credit
parts.note: read literally of a bank account: taking out more than is held leaves one in debit, not in credit

explanation.surface: Some action is said to reflect badly on whoever does it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'credit' looks like reputation but means the credit side of a bank balance.
explanation.definitionFit: Withdrawing more money than the account holds puts it into debit.

parts.note: the number written in figures is a single digit standing beside another of the same

explanation.walkthrough: Written as figures, 11 is a one placed by a one.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means singly in succession; the clue plays on the figures 1 and 1 side by side.

clue.text: A cry on the links and the rest is confusion

definitions.text: A cry on the links and the rest is confusion

parts.note: golfers shout 'fore' to warn people in the line of a shot

indicators.note: the word rest is thrown into confusion, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A golfer shouts a warning and everything after that is chaos.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf links supply FORE; 'is confusion' jumbles REST into STER. This old clue gives no separate definition: the whole clue stands for a woodsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodland keeper; the clue relies on the wordplay alone to point at the forest worker.

parts.note: read politically: the first, or Prime Minister, of those just elected in Labour's 1945 landslide

explanation.surface: A religious text speaks of the first among the chosen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the elect' sounds theological but means the newly elected Parliament; Clement Attlee became Prime Minister in 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: Clement Attlee led the Labour government formed after the 1945 general election, so he was the premier of the new House.

parts.note: a plain definition: to slander is to spread damaging falsehoods about someone

explanation.definitionFit: To cast false and damaging charges on a person's good name.

clue.text: One can wager on the steering-gear being wrong here

definitions.text: One can wager on the steering-gear being wrong here

parts.note: to wager is to bet

indicators.note: the word for the steering gear is put wrong, so its letters are disordered

parts.note: a ship's helm is its steering gear

explanation.surface: A punter bets on a ship's steering failing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being wrong' jumbles HELM into HLEM. Read whole, 'being wrong here' points to an old name for London's Bethlehem Hospital, the asylum for those whose minds had gone wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Bethlem was the London lunatic asylum, a place for the mentally disturbed.

parts.note: a medical-sounding phrase for those whose hearts are affected by love

explanation.surface: A doctor describes patients with a heart complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affection' sounds like a disease but means fondness; the heart is lovesick.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who worship or dote on someone have hearts touched by love.

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other, as the clue says it is found in the animals

parts.note: deer chew the cud, so are ruminants
encountered means met

explanation.surface: A goddess is spotted among grazing cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts MET inside DEER.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek deity of corn and harvest, mother of Persephone.

parts.note: the sheep that leads the flock wears a bell, so its lead is accompanied by ringing

explanation.surface: Something sets a resounding example for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ringing lead' sounds like a stirring example, but literally the leading sheep wears a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: The castrated ram wearing a bell that leads the flock, hence any leader or trend-setter.

clue.text: Those, of course, that every one of the animals named has

definitions.text: Those, of course, that every one of the animals named has

parts.words: Those, of course, that every one of the animals named has
parts.note: plays on the saying that every dog has its day, applied to the canine animals that name these hot weeks

explanation.surface: A writer notes what each of the animals mentioned possesses.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'every dog has its day' is the key; the hot weeks of high summer are named after the Dog Star.
explanation.definitionFit: The sultry weeks of midsummer, named for Sirius, the Dog Star.

indicators.note: the letters of the preceding words are made up into something else

explanation.surface: Craftsmen at the wheel are said to be so fabricated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'so made up' rearranges POTTERS ARE. This old clue gives no separate definition: the anagram alone points to a hunting weapon.
explanation.definitionFit: A barbed spear once used in hunting otters; the clue leaves the wordplay to point to it.

clue.text: As Anne seems to remark, a painter

indicators.note: what Anne seems to remark is heard rather than read, signalling a sound-alike

parts.note: to remark is to say, giving says
the name taken as written

explanation.surface: Anne apparently passes comment on an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Says Anne' spoken quickly gives the French painter's name; 'seems' signals the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Paul Cézanne was the French Post-Impressionist artist.

parts.note: refers to a poem by William Cowper titled The Progress of a mistake

explanation.surface: A literary note says some advance belongs to the poet Cowper.
explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper, the 18th-century English poet, wrote 'The Progress of Error'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mistake; Cowper's moral satire traces how a wrong spreads.

parts.note: an opera is a work of music

indicators.note: the word set is turned back to front

explanation.surface: A stage set is moved back to make room for the musicians.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns SET into TES after OPERA. The old clue gives no separate definition; the wordplay stands for the verb meaning works or runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Works or functions; the clue relies on the wordplay to lead to the verb.

parts.note: one who lives in a place rather than visiting it

explanation.definitionFit: A person who dwells in a place, as opposed to a visitor.

clue.text: Though untrue to begin with, it's high-toned

definitions.text: Though untrue to begin with, it's high-toned

parts.words: Though untrue to begin with, it's high-toned
parts.note: the word begins with a synonym of untrue and means a singing voice above the natural range

explanation.surface: Someone dishonest at first now behaves loftily.
explanation.walkthrough: The first five letters spell a word for untrue; 'high-toned' looks like snobbish but means high in pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's artificially high singing voice, above his natural register.

indicators.note: the letters of the first words are exchanged for a new word, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Gentle affection is set against brute strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' asks for NICE LOVE to be exchanged for a rearrangement; the surface contrast of love and force hides it.
explanation.definitionFit: Physical force used to hurt or damage is the core sense of the noun.

parts.note: a hen is a domestic fowl
the gist is the essence of a matter

explanation.surface: Chicken stock is offered to an invading army.
explanation.walkthrough: Hengist was the Jutish leader said to have invaded Britain in the fifth century.
explanation.definitionFit: Hengist led the Germanic settlers who, by tradition, conquered Kent around 450.

clue.text: This youngster, no doubt, sets a shining example

definitions.text: This youngster, no doubt, sets a shining example

parts.words: This youngster, no doubt, sets a shining example
parts.note: the lad who polishes footwear literally produces a shine

explanation.surface: A child is praised as a model for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shining example' sounds like praise but is literal: the boy shines shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy servant employed to clean and polish shoes in a hotel or school.

parts.note: the word means lovestruck, as worshippers are, but also literally struck, which they are not with blows

explanation.surface: A cross-reference says one group is something, though not with another.
explanation.walkthrough: 9 down are lovers, who are lovestruck; the word also means struck, which they are not with 31 across, blows.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeply in love, from an old past participle of smite, to strike.

parts.note: read literally: an adjective signifying belonging to the deep, the open sea

explanation.surface: Something is said to carry profound meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deep significance' suggests importance, but the word signifies 'of the deep sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to the open ocean, as distinct from coastal waters.

clue.text: Here one might find Eros in time

definitions.text: Here one might find Eros in time

indicators.note: the letters of the following words are found within the answer, rearranged

explanation.surface: A guide says that love's god may be found here eventually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Here one might find' signals that EROS IN TIME are rearranged. There is no separate definition: the hint is that great wrongs follow from love.
explanation.definitionFit: Monstrous wrongs or outrageous acts; the clue leaves the wordplay to point to them.

parts.note: a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A ban was imposed by the Greeks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was' is a link; the Greek is a native of Thebes.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Thebes, the ancient city of Boeotia.

clue.text: Joint finale, make no bones about it

definitions.text: Joint finale, make no bones about it

parts.words: Joint finale, make no bones about it
parts.note: the last of a roast joint is minced off the bone and fried in cakes

explanation.surface: Someone frankly announces the end of a partnership.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make no bones about it' sounds like 'speak frankly' but literally means boneless meat; 'Joint' is a roast of meat, not shared.
explanation.definitionFit: A fried cake of minced leftover meat, a thrifty end for a roast.

parts.note: a rotter is a scoundrel, and scoundrels are said to fall into ruin and vice

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that every cad behaves this way.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom means to fall into moral ruin; 'rotter' is old slang for a cad.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to fall into dissolute ways and be ruined.

indicators.note: to compose again is to put the letters together afresh in a new order

explanation.surface: A composer sets out to rework some melodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recompose' rearranges TUNES TO. The old clue gives no separate definition; the wordplay alone leads to the Germanic people.
explanation.definitionFit: Germanic peoples, from an ancient tribe; the clue leaves the anagram to point to them.

parts.note: a harbour that a mason might name: a haven of stone, located north of the border

explanation.surface: Freemasons gather in a Scottish harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Masonic' suggests Freemasons but just means made of stone; a haven is a port. Stonehaven is a town on the coast south of Aberdeen.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishing town and harbour in Aberdeenshire on Scotland's north-east coast.

clue.text: Punishment given by tigers to rabbits

definitions.meaning: blows of the cane given as a punishment
in golf a strong player (tiger) concedes handicap allowances to a weak one (rabbit)

explanation.surface: Big cats are said to punish bunnies.
explanation.walkthrough: In golf slang a 'tiger' is a strong player and a 'rabbit' a weak one; the better player gives the weaker extra shots as a handicap.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are blows or shots: cane lashes as a penalty, and handicap shots conceded in golf.
